concepts.label: evpn-instance
concepts.gloss: An EVPN instance is a provider-edge Layer-2 VPN service context that associates one or more attachment circuits and bridge domains with a common MAC-VRF and EVPN control-plane state.
concepts.example: EVI-5000 (MAC-VRF ACME) binds AC-PE1, AC-PE2, and AC-PE3 into the same EVPN service and carries bd-vlan-200.

concepts.label: attachment-circuit
concepts.gloss: An attachment circuit is the physical or logical provider-edge access connection through which a customer site or device enters a particular EVPN instance.
concepts.example: AC-PE1 is an access interface assigned to EVI-5000, allowing locally received customer Ethernet frames to enter the ACME MAC-VRF.

concepts.label: vpn-network-access
concepts.gloss: A VPN network access is the service-facing endpoint representing customer connectivity at a specific attachment circuit.
concepts.example: ep-PE1 represents the customer access endpoint located at AC-PE1, while ep-PE2 and ep-PE3 represent corresponding endpoints on the other attachment circuits.

concepts.label: bridge-domain
concepts.gloss: A bridge domain is an Ethernet broadcast and MAC-forwarding domain, commonly associated with a VLAN, that operates within an EVPN instance.
concepts.example: bd-vlan-200 is the VLAN 200 bridge domain in EVI-5000, within which Ethernet frames are bridged according to learned MAC destinations.

concepts.label: ingress-policer
concepts.gloss: An ingress policer is a rate-enforcement policy attached to an attachment circuit that meters arriving traffic and applies the configured conformance actions when its rate profile is exceeded.
concepts.example: policer-200/50 is applied on AC-PE1 so traffic entering EVI-5000 through that circuit is measured against the 200/50 rate profile.

concepts.label: traffic-class
concepts.gloss: A traffic class is a class-of-service category within an EVPN instance that groups packets or frames for a defined forwarding, queuing, or drop treatment.
concepts.example: In EVI-5000, traffic classified as EF-class receives the expedited-forwarding treatment, while traffic classified as BE-class receives best-effort treatment.

concepts.label: mac-vrf-learning
concepts.gloss: MAC-VRF learning is the local Layer-2 control function that learns source MAC addresses from frames received on an attachment circuit and installs their reachability in the associated MAC-VRF.
concepts.example: When a frame sourced by MAC 00:11:22:33:44:55 arrives on AC-PE1, local learning records that MAC as reachable through AC-PE1 in EVI-5000.

concepts.label: interface-mtu
concepts.gloss: An interface MTU is the maximum frame size configured for transmission or reception on an attachment circuit.
concepts.example: MTU 9100 on AC-PE1 permits Ethernet frames up to the configured 9,100-byte limit on that circuit and treats larger frames according to the interface's oversize-frame behavior.

concepts.label: ethernet-segment
concepts.gloss: An Ethernet segment is a customer Ethernet connection, identified by an Ethernet Segment Identifier, that can span attachment circuits on multiple provider edges for EVPN multihoming.
concepts.example: ESI-0011 identifies a dual-homed customer segment spanning AC-PE1 and AC-PE2, allowing EVPN procedures to coordinate forwarding and redundancy across both attachments.

concepts.label: MAC-mobility
concepts.gloss: MAC mobility is the EVPN control-plane mechanism that tracks a MAC address moving between attachment locations by advertising updated reachability with an increasing mobility sequence number.
concepts.example: After a MAC previously reachable through AC-PE1 appears behind AC-PE3, EVI-5000 advertises its new location with mobility sequence 3 so the newer route supersedes older reachability.
instances: mobility seq=3 for a moved MAC

concepts.label: vendor-evi-tag
concepts.gloss: A vendor EVI tag is opaque, implementation-specific metadata attached to an EVPN instance whose interpretation is defined by the vendor rather than by standard EVPN semantics.
concepts.example: EVI-5000 carries a vendor-evi-tag that the vendor's management or forwarding software consumes, while standards-based peers treat it as having no portable EVPN meaning.
